en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Drinking Liquor, 55.
The Training Rule on Terrifying Others:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were frightening the group-of-seventeen monks.
Being frightened, they wept.
The monks said this:
“Friends, why are you weeping?
“Friend, these monks of the group-of-six are terrifying us.
Those monks who were few in desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“How can the group of six monks actually frighten a monk? … [The Buddha said:
“Is it true, monks, that you are frightening a monk?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, frighten a bhikkhu?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whosoever monk should frighten another monk, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whosoever” means:
Whoever is such a one … [as described] … a bhikkhu … [and so on] … this is the meaning of "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"A nun" means another nun.
"Should frighten" means:

If one who is ordained, desiring to frighten another who is ordained, provides a form, sound, smell, taste, or tangible object; whether the other is frightened or not, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Or if he points out a wilderness infested with thieves, a wilderness infested with wild beasts, or a wilderness infested with malevolent spirits; whether the other is frightened or not, there is an offense of expiation.
If, regarding one who is ordained, he perceives them as ordained and frightens them, there is an offense of expiation.
If one causes someone who is fully ordained to be terrified while being in doubt [about their status], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one causes someone who is fully ordained to be terrified while perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation.
If, desiring to cause someone who is not fully ordained to be terrified, one presents a form, a sound, a smell, a taste, or a tangible object [to them].
Whether he fears it or not, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one points out a wilderness infested by thieves, a wilderness infested by wild beasts, or a wilderness infested by malevolent spirits,
whether he fears it or not, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, but one perceives them as ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the person] is not ordained, but one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, and one perceives them as not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

There is no offense if he does not bring about fear by presenting a form, sound, smell, taste, or tactile object; or if he points out a wilderness infested by thieves, a wilderness infested by wild beasts, or a wilderness infested by malevolent spirits;
or if he is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
the fifth training rule concerning frightening [others] is concluded.
